summary: Specifies how counter-based ciphers like AES-GCM, AES-CCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 in IPsec ESP can derive their initialization vector implicitly from the packet sequence number instead of sending it in every packet. This saves bytes per packet.

plainLanguage.summary: Two friends who count their messages together do not need to write the count on every note. Here the sender skips a number the receiver can work out itself.

questions: what is an implicit iv in esp
how to save bytes in ipsec esp packets
can implicit iv be used with multicast
what are the iiv ikev2 transform ids
subtitle: Saves 8 bytes per IPsec packet by building the cipher's IV from the sequence number instead of sending it.

tldr.problem: ESP sends an initialization vector (IV) in every packet, but for AES-GCM, AES-CCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 the IV only has to be unique, not secret or random, so sending it wastes bytes, which matters in contexts such as the Internet of Things.
tldr.mechanism: Both peers build the 8-byte IV locally from the ESP Sequence Number (padded with zeros, or the full Extended Sequence Number), and IKEv2 negotiates the new implicit-IV transforms alongside the explicit-IV ones.
tldr.outcome: Each packet is 8 octets smaller. The IV must never repeat for a key, so the SA has to be rekeyed before the sequence number would wrap.

today: RFC 8750 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of implicit IV for these ESP ciphers.

sections.title: Explicit and Implicit IVs
sections.content:
Counter-based modes such as AES-CCM (RFC 4309), AES-GCM (RFC 4106) and ChaCha20-Poly1305 (RFC 7634) need a nonce for each ESP packet. Today it is generated from an initialization vector carried in each ESP packet (RFC 4303). This document calls that an explicit IV.

In some settings, such as the Internet of Things, it is better not to carry those extra bytes and to generate the IV locally on each peer. That is an implicit IV. All the algorithms above take an 8-octet IV, and this document defines how to compute it and how peers agree on using it with IKEv2.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally every packet carries a little tag that the receiver needs. Here the receiver can rebuild the tag on its own, so the sender leaves it off.

sections.title: What Is Left Out
sections.content:
The scope is limited to AES-GCM, AES-CCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305. Other algorithms with similar properties may later use similar mechanisms.

AES-CBC (RFC 3602) is excluded because it needs an unpredictable IV. Deriving it from the packet counter is insecure and has led to real-world chosen plaintext attacks such as BEAST. AES-CTR (RFC 3686) is excluded because the document focuses on the recommended AEAD suites in RFC 8221.
sections.plainLanguage: This trick only works for ciphers where the tag just has to be different each time. For ciphers that need a surprising tag, a counting tag would be unsafe.

sections.title: How the Implicit IV Is Built
sections.content:
For these algorithms the 8-byte IV MUST NOT repeat for a given key. The binding between an ESP packet and its IV comes from the Sequence Number or the Extended Sequence Number.

  • With a regular 4-byte Sequence Number, the IV is a 4-byte Zero field followed by the 4-byte Sequence Number carried in the packet.
  • With an 8-byte Extended Sequence Number, the IV is that whole 8-byte number. Only its four low-order bytes are carried in the ESP packet.

Everything else about AES-GCM, AES-CCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 is unchanged and used as defined in their own specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag is just the packet's counter number, padded with zeros if it is short. Both sides know the counter, so both can make the same tag.

sections.title: Negotiating With IKEv2
sections.content:
An initiator that supports this feature SHOULD propose implicit IV (IIV) algorithms in the Transform Type 1 (Encryption Algorithm) substructure of the Proposal inside the SA payload. To stay compatible with peers that do not support it, the initiator SHOULD also offer the same algorithms with explicit IV as separate transforms.

The responder must pick from the initiator's proposal, so it never sends an SA payload containing an IIV transform to an initiator that did not propose one.
sections.plainLanguage: One side offers both the short way and the long way. The other side picks one from the offer, so nobody gets a surprise.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the IV must not repeat for one SA, implicit IV MUST NOT be used where the Sequence Number could overlap. Sender and receiver counters MUST be reset, by establishing a new SA and thus a new key, before the 2^32nd packet for an SA without an Extended Sequence Number, and before the 2^64th packet for an SA with one.

Multicast, where many senders share one secret and one SA, is a prominent example of trouble. Implicit IV may be used with multicast only if some mechanism prevents the Sequence Number from overlapping for the SA; otherwise it MUST NOT be used.

The new transforms are for ESP only and cannot be used in IKEv2, because IKEv2 messages have no unique per-message value to derive an IV from. The Message-ID resembles the ESP sequence number, but IKEv2 extensions allow it to repeat.
sections.plainLanguage: A tag must never be reused with the same key, so you switch to a fresh key before the counter runs out. Groups where many people send at once could repeat numbers, so extra care is needed there.

sections.title: New IKEv2 Transform IDs
sections.content: IANA added three code points to the Transform Type 1 (Encryption Algorithm) Transform IDs subregistry. They are defined for ESP, and IKEv2 use is marked not allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: Three new names were added to the official list, one for each cipher that can skip the tag.
